summary: Mali requires most visitors to obtain a visa in advance from an embassy, and Western governments advise against travel to most of the country; ECOWAS citizens have continued to enter visa-free under transitional arrangements despite Mali's January 2025 withdrawal from the bloc, and its Alliance of Sahel States partners Burkina Faso and Niger enjoy full free movement.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required of arriving travelers and is checked at Bamako airport; it is also requested with visa applications.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Mali

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not checked at the border, but comprehensive coverage including medical evacuation is essential — care in Bamako is limited and evacuation from Mali is complicated by the security situation.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Mali

onwardTicket.text: Not systematically checked, though visa applications ask for travel itineraries and airlines may ask for a return ticket.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Mali

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; officers may ask visitors to show sufficient means for their stay.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Mali

currencyLimits.text: Foreign currency should be declared on arrival; limits apply to exporting CFA francs. Confirm the current rules with a Malian embassy before carrying large sums.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Mali

payments.text: Mali is a cash economy. Cards work only at a few Bamako hotels and banks. Bring euros to exchange (the CFA franc is pegged to the euro) and carry enough cash for your whole stay.

safety.text: Mali is run by a military junta and large areas are affected by jihadist insurgency and armed conflict. Western governments advise against all travel to most of the country, including the north and center, and against all nonessential travel to Bamako — terrorism and kidnapping risks extend to the capital.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Mali Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to February is the cooler dry season and the only comfortable window — from March temperatures climb well above 40°C, and the June–September rains follow. Check security advice before planning any travel.

idp.text: Mali is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

tips.text: Most Western governments advise against all travel to northern and central Mali and against non-essential travel to the rest of the country, including Bamako — terrorism and kidnapping are real risks. Take professional security advice before any trip.

Mali formally left ECOWAS in January 2025 together with Burkina Faso and Niger, but visa-free entry for ECOWAS citizens has continued under transitional arrangements — West African travelers should re-confirm the rules shortly before traveling.
Do not photograph military personnel, checkpoints, government buildings or bridges — cameras and phones can be confiscated and detention is possible under the current military government.
Bring euros in cash. The CFA franc is pegged to the euro and exchanges easily in Bamako, while cards and ATMs cannot be relied on anywhere in the country.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Mali?
faq.answer: Most nationalities do. Visas must be obtained in advance from a Malian embassy, as there is no functioning eVisa or tourist visa on arrival. ECOWAS citizens continue to enter visa-free under transitional arrangements, and citizens of Burkina Faso and Niger move freely under the Alliance of Sahel States.

faq.question: Is Mali safe to visit?
faq.answer: No — most Western governments advise against travel to all or most of Mali. Jihadist insurgency affects the north and center, attacks and kidnappings have reached areas near Bamako, and the country is governed by a military junta. Any travel needs serious security planning.

faq.question: Can ECOWAS citizens still enter Mali visa-free?
faq.answer: In practice yes. Although Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger formally withdrew from ECOWAS in January 2025, both sides have kept visa-free movement for each other's citizens under transitional arrangements. The situation could change, so re-confirm shortly before travel.

faq.question: Can I get a visa on arrival in Mali?
faq.answer: No. There is no routine tourist visa on arrival and no eVisa. Apply at a Malian embassy before travel; where there is no Malian mission, a French or other partner embassy cannot issue Malian visas, so plan via the nearest embassy with jurisdiction.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination for Mali?
faq.answer: Yes. Carry an International Certificate of Vaccination. It is requested with visa applications and checked on arrival at Bamako-Sénou airport.
